items.title: Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
items.raw:
You can toggle through temperature settings directly from the mug, or from within the app. | Image: The Verge	

If you were cool on the $149.95 original price of the 14-ounce Ember Mug 3, you might warm up to the current discount happening at Amazon, Ember, and Best Buy for several colors of the (top rack) dishwasher-safe mug. It’s 33 percent off, dropping to $99.99 — still not cheap, but cheaper, and notably just $10 more than the 10-ounce version.
Ember Mug 3 (14 ounces)

Where to Buy:

 $149.95 $99.99 at Amazon
 $149.95 $99.99 at Best Buy
 $149.95 $99.99 at Ember

The Mug 3 affords you a couple of ways to control your drink’s temperature. A power button on the bottom of the mug can cycle between five temperature presets (125 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit), or you can use the app. It includes a sipping lid, and Ember claims that the Mug 3’s battery can keep drinks hot for up to three hours with the lid on. Without it, drinks stay hot for 80 minutes, the same battery claim as the Mug 2.
As we inch closer to the gift-getting season, the Ember Mug 3 seems like a solid product to snag for a coffee or tea lover who works from home, or for parents who have their hands full with kids and could always use a cuppa.

Some more great Verge-approved deals
Criterion Collection DVDs and Blu-rays are half off through December 6th at Amazon and Barnes and Noble, meaning you have plenty of time to assemble a wishlist of movies you want to buy ahead of the holiday season. The company’s catalog of films is vast, and it’s the best place to get limited edition releases of cherished films, old and new. Some of Criterion’s recent physical releases have been a hit, especially because they’ve quickly sunk in price. KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray is just $24.99 at Amazon and Barnes and Noble. Also, The Complete Kubrick boxset (currently the only way to get 4K Blu-ray versions of every one of the director’s legendary films) is half off, too, down to $299.99.
I’ve been wanting a USB-C cable that coils itself magnetically since my colleague Sean Hollister wrote about his favorites last year. That said, they tend to be a little pricey even if their tech specs are similar to cheaper cables, mostly due to the party trick. However, Werewolf (the company that makes the clever VFLEX for powering older gadgets via a USB-C power bank or wall charger) makes its own six-foot magnetic USB-C cable that’s just $12 right now (originally $27.50). It’s braided and supports up to 240W power passthrough, so it meets my criteria.
Google’s Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch is $100 off in both the Wi-Fi and LTE configurations at Amazon, though not all colors are included in the discount. The most affordable (and smallest) option is the 41mm Wi-Fi Pixel Watch 5, which costs $299.99. The larger 45mm watch face adds $30 to the price tag compared to the smaller version, whether you want Wi-Fi or LTE. One of the biggest improvements made to this generation is its GPS tracking. Google claims that it can outperform the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro — both of which cost a lot more — and we were impressed during our hands-on testing. Victoria Song tested it in the signal-congested West Village in Manhattan, walking in zigzags in an attempt to throw off the tracking. It wasn’t perfect, but it more accurately tracked turn-by-turn movement better than the Ultra 3. Read our review.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.
Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.
Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.
Allowing independent evaluation of their models.
Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.
Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.
But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.

items.title: Banana producers in Latin America want better pay to cope with effects of climate crisis
items.raw:
Farmers face big drop in production from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event
Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.

items.title: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 

 

 The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
